subject: Window seats with integrated storage
hook: A window seat only gets used if you plan it like a chair, not a shelf.
ig:
A window seat only gets used if you plan it like a chair, not a shelf.

Bay windows and deep reveals are perfect for a seat with storage underneath, but a few decisions make the difference between a reading spot and a cushion nobody sits on:

Height with the cushion on. Roughly dining-chair height is comfortable for most people.

Depth to sit back. Enough to lean against the wall or tuck your legs up.

Drawers or lift-up lids. Drawers open without moving the cushion; lids give deeper space for bulky things.

The radiator. If there's one below the window, the front needs ventilation so the heat still reaches the room.

The window itself. Handles, sills and blinds all need clearance.

Every window seat we make is measured to your window and built in our Hanley workshop.

on_asset:
S1: Window seats people actually sit on / Six things to plan before it's built |
S2: Count the cushion in the height — Seat height includes the cushion. Aim for roughly dining-chair height once it's on, or feet dangle and knees ache. |
S3: Deep enough to tuck your legs — Too shallow and it's a perch. Allow room to sit back against the wall or curl up sideways. |
S4: Drawers or lids, decided early — Drawers open without moving the cushion. Lift-up lids hold bulkier things but mean clearing the seat first. |
S5: Check the radiator — Many windows have one underneath. The front needs to let heat out, or that corner of the room goes cold. |
S6: Mind the window and blinds — Leave clearance for opening windows, handles, sills and blinds so the seat doesn't block them. |
